stories.headline: Global climate finance and action remain critical focus at COP31
stories.summary: COP31, meeting in Antalya, Türkiye, has reached its mid-point with nearly 200 governments still unable to explain how pledged climate action will be paid for. A draft agreement circulated at the summit urges countries to work back towards the 1.5°C goal and to accelerate the exit from fossil fuels, but developed and developing countries remain split over who should lead emission cuts and who should fund them. Western political attention has drifted from climate as the Trump administration has withdrawn international funding and the wars in Ukraine and West Asia have pushed up inflation and security spending. India has pressed an energy-security argument at the summit, with analysis showing that faster electrification could cut its fossil fuel import bill by more than 40% to ₹7.4 lakh crore by FY35, with transport offering the largest substitution opportunity. Outside the negotiating halls, civil society staged a global day of action in Antalya on November 14, widening the climate movement's demands beyond emissions.
stories.whyItMatters: COP31 is a live test of whether the Paris Agreement's finance and equity architecture — CBDR-RC, NDCs and the Loss and Damage fund — can actually deliver, a recurring theme in GS-III environment and GS-II global governance questions.

perspectives.take: Frames COP31 through geopolitics, arguing the US elections and the Iran war are shaping both the talks' atmosphere and the debate on fossil fuels; stresses a 'real-world impact' lens over pure diplomacy.

static.topic: Climate Change Regime & India's Commitments
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Climate Change
static.whatIsIt: The UNFCCC (1992) is the parent treaty; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015) operationalise it. India targets net-zero by 2070 and 50% installed non-fossil capacity by 2030.
static.background: Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR-RC) is the core equity principle. Paris uses NDCs and a ratchet mechanism. The Loss & Damage fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023). India leads the International Solar Alliance (2015) and the LiFE mission. COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, is the current round of this annual cycle, with a draft text calling for accelerated action to exit fossil fuels and a return towards 1.5°C.
static.geography: COP31 is hosted in Antalya, Türkiye, on the Mediterranean coast; the COP presidency rotates among UN regional groups, giving different regions agenda-setting influence.
static.socioEconomic: India's heavy fossil-fuel import dependence makes electrification both an energy-security and a current-account concern, while a just transition affects coal-dependent districts and livelihoods.
static.whyInNews: COP31's draft agreement and the persistent finance gap have refocused attention on whether NDCs, CBDR-RC and climate finance commitments can deliver the 1.5°C goal; India's electrification potential featured in summit-side analysis.
static.wayForward: Bridge the finance gap through predictable, grant-and-concessional flows, a credible post-2025 finance roadmap, MDB reform and technology transfer, while sequencing India's electrification with grid, storage and skilling investments.

stories.headline: Supreme Court suspends sentence, grants bail to two Bilkis Bano convicts
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has suspended the sentences of two men convicted in the Bilkis Bano gang rape case and granted them bail, more than 17 years after they were taken into custody. The order, published on the court's website, records that both had already undergone over 17 years of imprisonment and that one of them suffers from a severe handicap. Trial court records cited in reporting note that both were identified as part of the mob and that one lived across the street from the victim's house. The relief comes in a matter that has repeatedly returned to the apex court over the validity of the Gujarat government's 2022 remission order, which was quashed in January 2024. The court's reasoning rests on the length of incarceration already served rather than on any reconsideration of the conviction itself.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the balance between the Article 21 liberty of long-serving convicts and the gravity of heinous offences, and illustrates how closely the judiciary supervises state remission powers. Useful for questions on bail jurisprudence, sentencing policy and judicial review of executive clemency.

static.wayForward: Address judicial vacancies and pendency, balance judicial independence with accountability, and ensure reasoned orders are promptly made publicly accessible.

static.topic: Remission and Pardoning Powers in Criminal Justice

static.background: In January 2024 the Supreme Court quashed the Gujarat government's August 2022 remission order in the Bilkis Bano case, holding that the appropriate government to decide remission was Maharashtra, where the trial had been transferred and the conviction recorded. static.socioEconomic: Remission decisions sit at the intersection of victims' rights, retributive justice and the reformative theory of punishment.

static.wayForward: Codify clear and uniform remission guidelines, ensure victim participation and reasoned orders, and maintain transparent records of time actually served.

stories.headline: Nvidia board rules out Jensen Huang's return; Trump backs comeback bid
stories.summary: Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO, according to a source cited by CNBC and a Reuters report, even as a campaign for his reinstatement gains traction among some investors. US President Donald Trump said he 'would not mind' Huang being reinstated, remarking that Huang had 'learned a big lesson' and that a large group of people wanted him back, while dismissing espionage allegations that have swirled around the former chief. Separately reported accounts noted a sharp rise in the value of Trump's own Nvidia holdings as the controversy unfolded. The episode has divided investors and sharpened scrutiny of Nvidia's succession planning, and it runs alongside a parallel debate over whether export-banned Nvidia chips were used by China to train its most advanced AI models.
stories.whyItMatters: It links three recurring UPSC themes: the strategic weaponisation of semiconductor technology, the geopolitics of US export controls, and the governance standards expected of globally significant listed firms.

static.topic: India Semiconductor Mission and Domestic Chip Manufacturing
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — Industrial and Technological Development; Economy — Infrastructure
static.whatIsIt: A central mission under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) to build a semiconductor and display manufacturing ecosystem in India, offering fiscal support to fabrication plants, assembly-testing-marking-packaging (ATMP) and outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) units, and to chip design firms.
static.background: Announced in December 2021 with an outlay of about ₹76,000 crore under the Semicon India programme, with the India Semiconductor Mission set up as a dedicated division of MeitY. A Design Linked Incentive scheme supports domestic design startups, and the programme has drawn interest from global and Indian firms for fab and ATMP projects. India's earlier attempt, the Semiconductor Policy of 2007, had limited success.
static.geography: Proposed clusters span Dholera in Gujarat, Jagiroad in Assam, Noida in Uttar Pradesh, and locations in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu; fabs require ultra-pure water and uninterrupted power.
static.socioEconomic: Capital-intensive with long gestation periods; demands a large skilled workforce in electronics and materials engineering; expected to reduce import dependence for chips and create allied employment in testing, packaging and design services.
static.whyInNews: Global demand for AI accelerators and the churn in export-control policy have exposed how concentrated chip supply chains are, reinforcing the case for India's domestic capacity building.
static.wayForward: Build a talent pipeline in semiconductor engineering, deepen partnerships with global foundries and equipment makers, prioritise ATMP and compound semiconductors where entry barriers are lower, and align state incentives with the central mission.
prelimsPointers: The India Semiconductor Mission functions as a dedicated division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY).
ATMP stands for Assembly, Testing, Marking and Packaging — the back-end stage of chip manufacturing, distinct from front-end fabrication.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how global export controls and AI-driven chip demand affect India's semiconductor self-reliance ambitions and its position in global value chains.

static.topic: US Export Controls on Advanced Semiconductors and AI Chips
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of policies and politics of developed countries on India's interests; GS-III — Science & Technology
static.whatIsIt: Unilateral United States restrictions on the export of advanced computing chips, semiconductor manufacturing equipment and related technology to designated countries and entities, administered through the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Entity List.
static.background: Rooted in intensifying US–China technological competition, the controls progressively tightened the flow of advanced chips and tools to Chinese buyers. India and the US launched the Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology (iCET) in 2023 to deepen cooperation in semiconductors, AI and defence technology, while India has sought to gain from 'China plus one' supply-chain diversification.
static.geography: Global in scope; the critical chokepoints sit with design firms in the US, foundries in Taiwan and South Korea, lithography equipment suppliers in the Netherlands and specialty materials and tools suppliers in Japan.
static.socioEconomic: Determines access to AI compute, which in turn shapes data-centre costs, cloud services, research capacity and defence applications for third countries including India.
static.whyInNews: Reported questions over whether export-banned Nvidia chips were used to train China's most advanced AI models have revived the debate over how leakproof such controls really are.
static.wayForward: India needs diversified supply chains, domestic compute capacity such as the IndiaAI Mission's GPU procurement, and calibrated diplomacy that protects access to frontier technology without forfeiting strategic autonomy.
prelimsPointers: US export controls are administered by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) under the Department of Commerce.
The Wassenaar Arrangement is a multilateral export control regime covering conventional arms and dual-use goods and technologies.
India and the United States launched the Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology (iCET) in 2023.
static.mainsAngle: Semiconductors have become an instrument of strategic leverage. Discuss how US export controls affect the technology access and strategic autonomy of emerging economies such as India.

static.whatIsIt: The framework of board oversight, disclosure obligations, shareholder protection and succession planning that governs listed companies, anchored in the Companies Act, 2013 and the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015.
static.background: The Companies Act, 2013 strengthened board accountability by mandating independent directors and audit committees for prescribed classes of companies. static.whyInNews: The Nvidia board's stance on a CEO comeback, with investors openly divided, spotlights succession planning and the independence of boards from external political pressure.
static.wayForward: Companies should institutionalise written succession policies, preserve board independence, and disclose material leadership changes promptly; regulators should keep related-party and disclosure norms current.

stories.headline: Delhi seeks regional air pollution strategy with World Bank
stories.summary: The Delhi government is in talks with the World Bank to adopt an airshed-based approach that would coordinate pollution-control measures across neighbouring states, moving beyond city-centric curbs. The shift comes as Delhi's air quality remains 'poor' with an AQI of 216 and Stage III GRAP restrictions continue. In parallel, the Supreme Court has called for an encroachment-free Yamuna floodplain and penalties on states over pollution, while AISA chief Neha and cancer patients protested in Delhi demanding stronger action. Newslaundry reports highlight the broader air pollution crisis and the repeated failure to clean the Yamuna despite large expenditures.

stories.headline: RBI presses Tata Sons on listing as Tata family rift widens
stories.summary: The Reserve Bank of India has reiterated its demand that Tata Sons, the holding company of the Tata group, be listed on stock exchanges — a requirement that flows from the central bank's Scale Based Regulation framework for non-banking financial companies placed in the 'upper layer'. The regulatory push has become entangled with a public family dispute: Jimmy N Tata, half-brother of the late Ratan Tata, has backed the listing and accused his half-brother Noel Tata of engineering a 'back-door takeover' of Tata Sons by packing the Tata Trusts with family members. Noel Tata chairs the Trusts, which hold a majority stake in Tata Sons. The Indian Express reports that the RBI's reiteration leaves the company little room to manoeuvre, while Business Standard foregrounds the argument that listing is critical to dismantling a culture of secrecy.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests how far prudential regulation can reach into a privately held holding company, and raises questions about governance and accountability in promoter-controlled charitable trusts. Directly relevant to GS-III questions on NBFC regulation, corporate governance and capital markets.

static.topic: RBI's Scale Based Regulation and the listing requirement for upper-layer NBFCs
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking & Monetary Policy / Regulation of Non-Banking Financial Companies
static.whatIsIt: The RBI is India's central bank and principal financial-sector regulator, established in 1935 (nationalised 1949) under the RBI Act, 1934. Besides monetary policy, it regulates banks and non-banking financial companies, including Core Investment Companies (CICs) such as Tata Sons. Under its Scale Based Regulation (SBR) framework, NBFCs are graded into Base, Middle, Upper and Top layers, with progressively stricter compliance — including a mandatory stock-exchange listing for entities placed in the upper layer.
static.background: The RBI Act, 1934 created the RBI; it was nationalised in 1949. Monetary policy is conducted through the six-member Monetary Policy Committee, instituted in 2016 with a 4% CPI inflation target (±2%). On the regulatory side, the RBI replaced its older asset-size-based classification of NBFCs with the four-tier Scale Based Regulation framework, announced in October 2021, which requires upper-layer NBFCs to list within a stipulated period of being notified. Tata Sons is registered with the RBI as a Core Investment Company — a category of NBFC whose assets are overwhelmingly investments in group companies.
static.socioEconomic: Listing would bring a large, closely held group holding company under public disclosure norms, potentially widening retail participation and subjecting related-party dealings and promoter holdings to market scrutiny.
static.whyInNews: The RBI has reiterated its demand that Tata Sons comply with the listing requirement applicable to upper-layer NBFCs, a position that leaves the company limited room to manoeuvre.
static.wayForward: Tata Sons must either comply with the listing requirement within the RBI's timeline or seek a legally sustainable exemption; the RBI, for its part, must ensure that the SBR framework is applied consistently across upper-layer entities so that regulatory credibility is not diluted.
prelimsPointers: The RBI's Scale Based Regulation framework (2021) classifies NBFCs into four layers — Base, Middle, Upper and Top — with upper-layer entities required to list on stock exchanges.
A Core Investment Company is an NBFC whose assets are predominantly investments in group companies; Tata Sons is registered with the RBI in this category.
The RBI was established in 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934 and nationalised in 1949.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether mandatory listing of upper-layer NBFCs is an effective prudential tool or an excessive intrusion into promoter autonomy, using the Tata Sons case as an illustration.

static.topic: Corporate governance, mandatory listing and promoter-controlled holding structures
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Corporate Governance and Capital Markets
static.whatIsIt: Corporate governance in India rests on the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI's Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements (LODR) Regulations, which impose disclosure, board-composition and related-party-transaction norms on listed entities. Because these obligations attach mainly to listed companies, a privately held holding company can control a large listed group while itself remaining largely exempt from public disclosure.
static.background: SEBI's Committee on Corporate Governance, chaired by Uday Kotak (2017), recommended tighter norms on board independence, related-party transactions and promoter shareholding, many of which were subsequently notified through amendments to the LODR Regulations. The Tata group's ownership architecture — in which the Tata Trusts, a set of philanthropic trusts, hold a majority stake in Tata Sons, which in turn controls the listed operating companies — has long been cited as an example of a structure where control and disclosure are separated.
static.socioEconomic: Philanthropic trusts holding controlling stakes in large business groups raise questions about accountability: trust decisions affect listed companies, minority shareholders and employees, yet trust governance is not subject to the same market discipline as listed entities.
static.whyInNews: The listing demand has become the pivot of a public dispute within the Tata family, with allegations that the Trusts are being packed with family members to consolidate control — a charge that goes to the heart of governance in promoter-controlled structures.
static.wayForward: Strengthening disclosure and governance standards for unlisted holding companies and for trusts that exercise control over listed entities would address the regulatory gap without necessarily forcing a change in ownership.
prelimsPointers: SEBI's LODR Regulations govern disclosure and governance obligations of listed companies.
The Kotak Committee (2017) on corporate governance recommended reforms on board independence and related-party transactions.
The Companies Act, 2013 is the principal statute governing incorporation, management and winding up of companies in India.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether India's corporate governance framework adequately addresses unlisted holding companies and controlling trusts that exercise decisive influence over listed firms.

prelims: The RBI's Scale Based Regulation framework (2021) places NBFCs in Base, Middle, Upper and Top layers; upper-layer NBFCs are required to list on stock exchanges.
Tata Sons is registered with the RBI as a Core Investment Company — an NBFC whose assets are predominantly investments in group companies.
The Tata Trusts hold a majority stake in Tata Sons, which is the holding company of the listed Tata group companies.

stories.mainsQuestion: The RBI's insistence on the listing of Tata Sons highlights the tension between prudential regulation of non-banking financial companies and the autonomy of promoter-controlled holding structures. stories.headline: US Supreme Court Blocks Trump's Bid to Cancel 'DEI' Research Grants
stories.summary: The US Supreme Court declined to let the Trump administration cancel billions of dollars in federal research grants that it had classified as 'DEI programs', leaving intact a lower court ruling that the administration was probably acting illegally. The decision is a setback to the White House's broader campaign against diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives across the federal government. CalMatters reported that the outcome directly affects University of California researchers who had faced the prospect of losing funding. Separately, Scroll.in used the wider US political context, including Democratic gains in the midterms, to argue that India's opposition lacks a comparable capacity to produce electoral upsets. Together the coverage frames the ruling as both a legal check on executive power and a flashpoint in the comparative politics of affirmative action.
stories.whyItMatters: For UPSC, the ruling illustrates judicial review of executive action, separation of powers and the constitutional limits on grant-making discretion. It also feeds the comparative debate on affirmative action and DEI, which is directly relevant to India's reservation jurisprudence under Articles 15 and 16.

static.topic: Judicial Review and Checks on Executive Action
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary
static.whatIsIt: Judicial review is the power of courts to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution. In India, the Supreme Court (Article 124) and High Courts (Article 214) exercise this power, with writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226.
static.background: The doctrine traces to Marbury v Madison (1803) in the US. In India, Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine, while the collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s.
static.whyInNews: The US Supreme Court declined to allow the Trump administration to cancel federal research grants it labelled DEI, leaving intact a lower court ruling that the administration probably acted illegally.
static.wayForward: Strengthen judicial capacity to handle executive-action litigation, reduce pendency and vacancies, and maintain a principled balance between judicial independence and accountability.
prelimsPointers: Article 32 provides writ jurisdiction to the Supreme Court; Article 226 to High Courts.
Original jurisdiction over Centre-state disputes lies with the Supreme Court under Article 131.
Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is under Article 143.
static.mainsAngle: Examine judicial review as a check on executive overreach in grant-making and policy implementation, and assess the balance between judicial independence and accountability in India.

static.topic: Affirmative Action and DEI: Comparative Constitutional Context
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Social Justice and Reservation
static.whatIsIt: Affirmative action and diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies aim to redress historical disadvantage in education, employment and public funding. In India, this operates through Articles 15(4) and 16(4) and related reservation provisions.
static.background: In the US, Executive Order 11246 (1965) mandated affirmative action in federal contracting; Regents of the University of California v Bakke (1978) shaped race-conscious admissions, and Students for Fair Admissions v Harvard/UNC (2023) curtailed them. In India, the Mandal Commission led to OBC reservations, Indra Sawhney (1992) upheld a 50% ceiling, and the 103rd Amendment (2019) introduced EWS reservation.
static.socioEconomic: DEI debates intersect with representation in higher education, research funding and employment, and with questions of merit versus equity in public resource allocation.
static.whyInNews: The US Supreme Court blocked the Trump administration's attempt to cancel federal grants it classified as DEI, keeping funding for research projects intact.
static.wayForward: Design inclusion policies that are evidence-based, constitutionally sound and periodically reviewed, while ensuring they do not become instruments of political retribution.
prelimsPointers: Indra Sawhney (1992) upheld OBC reservation and a 50% ceiling, excluding the 'creamy layer'.
The 103rd Constitutional Amendment (2019) introduced 10% EWS reservation.
In the US, Students for Fair Admissions v Harvard/UNC (2023) restricted race-conscious admissions.
static.mainsAngle: Compare India's reservation jurisprudence with US affirmative action and DEI debates, and evaluate how courts balance merit, equity and executive discretion in funding decisions.

prelims: The US Supreme Court declined to allow the Trump administration to cancel billions of dollars in federal research grants it had labelled 'DEI programs'.
A lower court ruling that the administration was probably acting illegally in targeting such research projects remains intact.
CalMatters reported that the outcome directly affects University of California researchers who faced potential funding loss.
The case is a live example of judicial review of executive action in the US, comparable in principle to Indian writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226.
stories.mainsQuestion: Judicial review of executive action is a cornerstone of constitutional checks and balances. Discuss this in the light of recent US Supreme Court rulings on DEI-related federal grants, and draw comparative lessons for India's separation-of-powers and affirmative-action debates.

stories.headline: US-China-Russia Shenzhen Summit Frames Global Order, Nuclear Risks
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin met in Shenzhen during Trump's wider Asia trip, which also produced deals in Manila and Shenzhen and a possible meeting with Kim Jong Un. Beijing highlighted the meeting's significance, while reports said the agenda covered Russia's war in Ukraine, West Asia and stabilising global energy supplies, and nuclear arms control. Analysts cited in the coverage suggest the meeting may be more symbolic than substantive, with few enforceable outcomes expected. The Indian Express editorialises that these overlapping Asia summits frame India's own stakes in a shifting great-power order. India Global Review frames the encounter as a possible 'Yalta 2.0' and asks what Trump wants from it.

static.topic: United Nations and Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance
static.whatIsIt: The UN, founded in 1945, has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members and ten elected members. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion. Intergovernmental Negotiations on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.whyInNews: A US-China-Russia summit in Shenzhen brings P5 dynamics into focus, raising questions about whether great-power concerts can bypass or reshape UN-centred multilateralism.

static.topic: Nuclear Arms Control and Strategic Stability
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Nuclear Diplomacy and Arms Control
static.whatIsIt: Nuclear arms control refers to treaties and mechanisms to limit, reduce or verify nuclear weapons. Key instruments include the NPT, CTBT, IAEA safeguards and bilateral US-Russia accords.
static.background: The NPT opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970; India is not a party. The CTBT, adopted in 1996, bans explosive nuclear testing but has not entered into force, and India has not signed it. The IAEA verifies safeguards.
static.whyInNews: The Shenzhen summit's reported agenda includes nuclear arms control amid US-China-Russia strategic competition.
static.wayForward: India should monitor great-power arms control talks for implications on strategic stability, while maintaining credible minimum deterrence and no-first-use.

CTBT adopted in 1996 has not entered into force; India has not signed it.

stories.headline: Third US carrier enters West Asia as Yemen war reignites
stories.summary: The USS Theodore Roosevelt has arrived in West Asia, restoring the US carrier presence in the region to three — an unusually high concentration — as Washington keeps its options open in its confrontation with Iran. In parallel, the renewed US-Iran hostilities have re-energised Yemen's frozen civil war, with the Houthis making rapid gains against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Riyadh has responded to the setback by replacing its military commander, signalling a return to direct confrontation with the group. Together the two developments point to a widening, interlinked conflict theatre spanning the Gulf, the Red Sea and the Bab-el-Mandeb approaches.
stories.whyItMatters: West Asia is India's principal energy source and home to a large diaspora; escalation involving the US, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the Houthis directly affects oil prices, shipping lanes and India's connectivity projects. It is also a live test of UNSC efficacy and of India's strategic-autonomy balancing.

static.topic: US Military Presence in West Asia and Gulf Security Architecture
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its neighbourhood; effect of policies of developed and developing countries on India's interests
static.whatIsIt: The forward deployment of US naval and air assets — notably aircraft carrier strike groups — in West Asia, anchored on the US Central Command (CENTCOM) area of responsibility and the US Fifth Fleet based in Bahrain.
static.background: The US has maintained a continuous naval presence in the Gulf since the 1949 establishment of a Middle East force and the 1971 creation of the Fifth Fleet's predecessor command; the Fifth Fleet was re-established in 1995. Carrier deployments have historically been used as signalling instruments during crises with Iran, including repeated Strait of Hormuz episodes. The 2020s saw episodic surges in carrier numbers during Israel-Hamas and Red Sea shipping crises.
static.geography: Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz, Gulf of Oman, Red Sea and Bab-el-Mandeb — the chokepoints through which a large share of global seaborne crude and India-bound energy cargo passes.
static.socioEconomic: Carrier surges raise war-risk insurance premiums, reroute shipping and feed directly into crude prices, transmitting into India's import bill, current account and inflation.
static.whyInNews: A third US aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, has arrived in West Asia, an unusually high concentration, as Washington keeps options open in its conflict with Iran.
static.wayForward: India's interest lies in de-escalation and freedom of navigation; it must balance its deepening US defence partnership with its energy and connectivity ties to Gulf states and its historical relationship with Iran.
prelimsPointers: The US Fifth Fleet is headquartered in Bahrain; CENTCOM's headquarters is in Tampa, Florida.
The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and is the world's most critical oil chokepoint.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how great-power military posturing in West Asia affects India's energy security, diaspora safety and strategic autonomy.

static.topic: Yemen Civil War and the Houthi Insurgency
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests; regional conflicts
static.whatIsIt: A multi-sided civil war in Yemen pitting the Iran-aligned Houthi movement against the internationally recognised Yemeni government backed by a Saudi-led coalition, with southern separatist forces and jihadist groups as additional actors.
static.background: The Houthis, a Zaidi Shia revivalist movement from the Saada governorate in northern Yemen, seized Sana'a in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition intervention in March 2015. The conflict has since been described by the UN as one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. A UN-brokered nationwide truce in 2022 substantially reduced front-line fighting but did not produce a durable political settlement, leaving the war frozen rather than resolved.
static.geography: Yemen sits at the south-western tip of the Arabian Peninsula, bordering Saudi Arabia and Oman and commanding the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez route.
static.socioEconomic: Prolonged conflict has produced mass displacement, famine risk and near-total dependence on imported food and fuel; Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping have raised global freight and insurance costs.
static.whyInNews: The Houthis have made rapid gains against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government since the US-Iran conflict reignited Yemen's frozen civil war, prompting Saudi Arabia to replace its military commander.
static.wayForward: A durable settlement requires an inclusive, UN-led Yemeni political process, humanitarian access guarantees and regional de-escalation between Riyadh and Tehran; military reorganisation alone cannot substitute for a political track.
prelimsPointers: The Houthis belong to the Zaidi branch of Shia Islam and are based in northern Yemen's Saada governorate.
Bab-el-Mandeb lies between Yemen and Djibouti/Eritrea and links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how the Yemen conflict illustrates the linkage between regional proxy rivalries and global maritime security, and assess India's stakes in Red Sea stability.

static.topic: UN Security Council Reform and the P5 Veto
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Important International institutions, agencies and fora: their structure, mandate
static.whatIsIt: The UN Security Council is the primary organ responsible for international peace and security, with five permanent veto-wielding members and ten elected members serving two-year terms.
static.background: The UN was founded in 1945 with six principal organs. India is a founding member and among the largest troop contributors to UN peacekeeping. The G4 — India, Brazil, Germany and Japan — campaigns for permanent membership and expansion. The Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) process on Security Council reform remains inconclusive, with the African Ezulwini Consensus and the veto question as central sticking points.
static.whyInNews: Repeated veto-driven paralysis in the Security Council over West Asian conflicts — including Iran and Yemen — renews the debate on Council reform and the representativeness of the P5.
static.wayForward: India's case rests on representativeness, population and peacekeeping contributions; progress requires bridging the veto question and the divergent positions of the African group, the Uniting for Consensus bloc and the P5 themselves.
prelimsPointers: The UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent and 10 elected for two-year terms.
The International Court of Justice sits at The Hague; the UN headquarters is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether the UN Security Council's structure is adequate to address contemporary West Asian conflicts, and evaluate India's claim to permanent membership.

stories.headline: BJP's Bengal unit in turmoil: worker's murder, defection backlash, factional feuds
stories.summary: Two incidents in West Bengal's North 24 Parganas have brought factional friction inside the State BJP into the open: a party worker, Arup Saha, was killed in Panihati in an attack attributed to fellow party members, and Union Minister and Bongaon MP Santanu Thakur alleged that BJP workers are being assaulted by their own colleagues while the police administration remains passive. The local MLA publicly said she felt personally responsible for the worker's death, and sections of the party's ranks demanded an end to inducting former Trinamool Congress members, blaming rapid recruitment for the unrest. Separately, a Murshidabad BJP leader has proposed a 'rulebook' for the party in the State that would bar informal forms of address such as 'boudi' and 'bondhu' in favour of a stricter social code. National commentary has linked these strains to wider organisational disarray, with one report describing internal mistrust over candidate selection ahead of the Uttar Pradesh polls.

static.topic: Internal Democracy in Political Parties
static.syllabusNode: Polity and Governance — Political Parties, Representation of the People Act, Electoral Reforms
static.whatIsIt: Internal democracy refers to transparent, rule-bound functioning within political parties — periodic organisational elections, fair candidate selection, inclusive decision-making and grievance redress — as envisaged in party constitutions and the conditions attached to registration with the Election Commission of India.
static.background: Political parties are registered with the ECI under Section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (inserted in 1989), which requires a party to subscribe to a written constitution and to abide by the Constitution of India and the principles of socialism, secularism and democracy. The ECI's 2002 order required registered parties to hold organisational elections and file audited accounts annually. The Law Commission's 170th Report (1999) on reform of electoral laws and the 255th Report (2015) on electoral reforms recommended measures to strengthen inner-party democracy and regulate party functioning and funding.
static.geography: West Bengal — the reported factional contests are located in North 24 Parganas (Panihati, Bongaon) and Murshidabad district.
static.socioEconomic: Factions typically coalesce around patronage networks, local strongmen and access to tickets, posts and contracts; the rapid induction of rival-party cadres can sharpen competition for these resources and alienate older workers.
static.whyInNews: A BJP worker's killing in Panihati, a Union Minister's allegation that BJP workers are being attacked by fellow party members, and a proposed conduct 'rulebook' in Murshidabad have all been reported as signs of weak internal discipline and factionalism in the State unit.
static.wayForward: Codify and enforce organisational elections, publish transparent criteria for tickets and inductions, create internal dispute-resolution mechanisms, and strengthen ECI oversight of party constitutions and accounts so that cadre grievances are channelled institutionally rather than through violence.
prelimsPointers: Political parties are registered with the ECI under Section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
The ECI's 2002 order requires registered parties to hold organisational elections and submit audited accounts annually.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why internal democracy in Indian political parties remains weak despite statutory and ECI requirements, and assess how far inner-party reform can curb factionalism and cadre violence.

static.topic: Anti-Defection Law and Cross-Party Inductions
static.syllabusNode: Polity and Governance — Parliament and State Legislatures, Tenth Schedule
static.whatIsIt: The Tenth Schedule disqualifies a legislator who voluntarily gives up membership of a party or votes/abstains against the party whip; the presiding officer of the House decides on disqualification, and a merger is protected only if at least two-thirds of a legislature party agrees to it.
static.background: The Tenth Schedule was inserted by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985. The 91st Amendment Act, 2003 deleted the earlier exemption for a split by one-third of the members of a legislature party. In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court upheld the validity of the Tenth Schedule while holding the Speaker's decision subject to judicial review.
static.socioEconomic: Cross-party migration of leaders and cadres is common in competitive State contests; it can boost a party's immediate strength while generating resentment among long-standing workers who see tickets and influence being handed to newcomers.
static.whyInNews: After the Panihati killing, sections of the BJP's ranks publicly demanded that the party stop inducting former Trinamool Congress members, linking the unrest to rapid recruitment from a rival party.
static.wayForward: Strengthen transparency in membership drives and ticket allocation, consider independent adjudication of defection petitions, and build internal mechanisms to absorb new entrants without displacing existing cadre.
prelimsPointers: The Tenth Schedule was inserted by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985.
The 91st Amendment Act, 2003 removed the one-third split exemption; only a merger supported by two-thirds of a legislature party is protected.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether the anti-defection law has been effective in curbing political defection, and examine the relationship between mass cross-party induction and intra-party instability.

static.topic: Political Violence and Criminalisation of Politics
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Law and Order, Criminalisation of Politics, Role of Police
static.whatIsIt: Political violence covers clashes among party cadres and attacks on party workers, while criminalisation of politics refers to persons with criminal antecedents contesting and entering legislatures; both implicate the impartiality of the police and the integrity of electoral processes.
static.background: Following the Supreme Court's judgment in Public Interest Foundation v. Union of India (2018), candidates must declare their criminal antecedents in their nomination affidavits (Form 26), and political parties are required to publish on their websites and in newspapers the reasons for selecting candidates with criminal antecedents. Election-time conduct is regulated by the Model Code of Conduct enforced by the ECI, while law-and-order maintenance is a State subject under the police and public order entries of the State List.
static.geography: West Bengal has witnessed recurring cadre clashes; the incidents reported here relate to Panihati and Bongaon in North 24 Parganas district.
static.socioEconomic: Localised political competition, patronage over contracts and municipal bodies, and dense party networks in urban and semi-urban areas can make cadre-level disputes escalate into violence.
static.whyInNews: A Union Minister alleged that the police administration in West Bengal is not functioning impartially in cases where BJP workers are attacked by fellow party members, raising questions about neutral enforcement of law and order.
static.wayForward: Ensure prompt, impartial investigation of political violence, strengthen police accountability mechanisms, enforce disclosure norms for candidates with criminal antecedents, and reduce the incentive for violence through transparent local governance.
keyTerms: Public Interest Foundation v. Union of India (2018)
State List — police and public order
prelimsPointers: Candidates must disclose criminal antecedents in Form 26 affidavits; the 2018 Supreme Court ruling required parties to publicise why such candidates were fielded.
'Police' and 'public order' are entries in the State List of the Seventh Schedule.
static.mainsAngle: Political violence among party cadres undermines the neutrality of the State apparatus. Analyse the causes and suggest institutional safeguards to ensure impartial law enforcement during political conflict.

prelims: The Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment Act, 1985) disqualifies legislators for defection; the 91st Amendment Act, 2003 removed the one-third split exemption.
Political parties are registered with the Election Commission of India under Section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
Panihati and Bongaon are in North 24 Parganas district, West Bengal; Murshidabad is a separate district in the State.

stories.mainsQuestion: Intra-party factionalism and cadre violence are increasingly visible in Indian politics. Examine the causes of such feuds and evaluate whether stronger internal democracy in political parties can address them.

stories.headline: JPMorgan software bug disrupts US banking; Microsoft flags server failures
stories.summary: A software defect at JPMorgan Chase disrupted online banking for customers across several large US banks, with users reporting difficulty logging in and accessing accounts. Outage-tracking site Downdetector listed Bank of America, Chase, J.P. Morgan, U.S. Bank, Wells Fargo and the payments network Zelle among the services showing problems. JPMorgan attributed the disruption to a software bug that slowed transaction processing, and the technical issue cascaded into delays at other institutions connected to the same payment rails. Separately, Microsoft said that more than 80% of its servers failed during a global outage, which it linked to a software bug dating from July. Together the episodes point to the concentration and interconnection risk in digital financial and cloud infrastructure.
stories.whyItMatters: Banking and cloud outages are a live case study on operational risk, critical information infrastructure and third-party concentration risk — themes that recur in GS-III economy, internal security and disaster-management questions.

perspectives.take: Frames it as a consumer-facing service failure, using Downdetector user reports to show the breadth of banks and payment apps affected.
Traces the disruption to a single technical issue at JPMorgan Chase and highlights the knock-on delays at other major US banks.
Shifts focus to the cloud layer, reporting Microsoft's claim that over 80% of servers failed in a global outage blamed on a July software bug.
Business-wire framing centred on corporate confirmation — JPMorgan's own statement that a software bug slowed its transactions.

static.topic: Critical Information Infrastructure (CII) Protection in India
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Cyber Security and Critical Infrastructure Protection
static.whatIsIt: Critical Information Infrastructure means a computer resource whose incapacitation would destroy or severely damage national security, the economy, public health or public safety. Banking, payments, power, telecom and transport systems are treated as CII, and their protection is coordinated by designated national agencies.
static.background: The legal basis is the Information Technology Act, 2000. The IT (Amendment) Act, 2008 inserted Section 70A, under which the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC) was set up as the nodal agency for CII protection, becoming operational in 2014. Section 70B designates the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), established in 2004, as the national nodal agency for responding to cyber security incidents. Both function under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology.
static.socioEconomic: India's high dependence on real-time digital payments means even short outages can stall wages, small-merchant sales and welfare transfers, disproportionately affecting low-income users who have no cash fallback.
static.whyInNews: Simultaneous outages at major US banks and at Microsoft's server fleet illustrate how a single software defect in a concentrated digital system can disrupt millions of users.
static.wayForward: Periodic CII audits, mandatory incident reporting within tight timelines, sectoral CERTs, redundancy and failover testing, and drills that simulate multi-institution failure rather than single-firm failure.
prelimsPointers: CERT-In is the national nodal agency for cyber incident response under Section 70B of the IT Act; NCIIPC is the CII nodal agency under Section 70A.
Both agencies operate under MeitY; NCIIPC identifies CII across power, banking and finance, telecom, transport, government and strategic sectors.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether India's critical information infrastructure protection framework is adequate for a digital economy where a single vendor or software defect can cause system-wide disruption.

static.topic: Operational Risk and Business Continuity in Banking
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Banking, Financial Sector and Financial Stability
static.whatIsIt: Operational risk is the risk of loss arising from inadequate or failed internal processes, people, systems or from external events. IT and software failures, cyber attacks and vendor outages fall squarely within it, alongside fraud and legal risk.
static.background: Operational risk was formalised as a distinct regulatory risk category under the Basel framework, alongside credit and market risk. In India, the Reserve Bank of India has issued a cyber security framework for banks and directions on IT governance, risk, controls and assurance, requiring board-level oversight, business continuity plans and periodic resilience testing. Retail payment systems such as UPI are operated by the National Payments Corporation of India, an umbrella organisation for retail payments promoted by the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association.
static.socioEconomic: Because a handful of banks, payment networks and cloud providers sit beneath most digital transactions, third-party concentration risk converts a firm-level technical fault into a public-utility-style failure.
static.whyInNews: A JPMorgan software bug slowed transactions and disrupted online banking at several large US banks, showing how operational failure at one node propagates across the payment chain.
static.wayForward: Stronger third-party and cloud concentration limits, mandatory recovery-time and recovery-point objectives, independent resilience testing, and clear customer compensation norms for prolonged outages.
prelimsPointers: Operational risk is treated as a distinct risk category alongside credit and market risk under the Basel framework.
NPCI is the umbrella organisation for retail payments in India, promoted by the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how rising dependence on a few technology vendors and cloud providers is reshaping operational risk in banking, and evaluate the adequacy of existing prudential safeguards.

static.topic: Global Governance of Cyberspace and Multilateral Cooperation
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance and Multilateral Institutions
static.whatIsIt: There is no single global treaty governing cyberspace. Norms are developed through UN processes — the Group of Governmental Experts (GGE) and the Open-Ended Working Group (OEWG) — while the Council of Europe's Budapest Convention is the principal international treaty on cybercrime.
static.background: UN expert processes on information and communication technology security have met since the mid-2000s; their consensus reports affirmed that international law, including the UN Charter, applies to cyberspace and set out voluntary norms of responsible state behaviour. The OEWG format was created to allow all UN member states, not just a small expert group, to participate. India engages in these processes and has consistently argued for a multilateral, UN-centred approach to cyber governance.
static.socioEconomic: Cross-border cloud and payment infrastructure means an outage or attack in one jurisdiction is felt immediately in others, creating demand for shared incident reporting and mutual assistance norms.
static.whyInNews: Simultaneous banking and cloud outages across countries underline the absence of binding international mechanisms for cross-border digital resilience and accountability.
static.wayForward: Strengthen confidence-building measures, capacity building for developing countries, and sector-specific cooperation on financial and cloud infrastructure resilience within UN-led frameworks.
prelimsPointers: The Budapest Convention, adopted under the Council of Europe in 2001, is the first international treaty addressing cybercrime.
UN GGE reports affirmed that international law and the UN Charter apply to state behaviour in cyberspace.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether the existing UN-led, norm-based architecture for cyberspace is sufficient to manage the systemic risks created by globally concentrated digital infrastructure.

prelims: Downdetector is a crowd-sourced website that tracks user-reported outages of internet services, banks and payment platforms.
Zelle is a US peer-to-peer payments network operated by a consortium of banks, distinct from card networks.
CERT-In (Section 70B, IT Act) handles cyber incident response, while NCIIPC (Section 70A) protects critical information infrastructure in India.
Operational risk — covering system and process failures — is a distinct regulatory risk category alongside credit and market risk under the Basel framework.
stories.mainsQuestion: Software failures at a few large technology and financial firms can quickly cascade into system-wide disruption. Examine the risks this poses to India's digital financial infrastructure and suggest measures to strengthen operational resilience.

stories.headline: ECI tells Supreme Court SIR was unanimous; no prosecution for Form 6 voters
stories.summary: The Election Commission has told the Supreme Court that no criminal prosecution will follow against voters whose names were deleted during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) if they apply afresh through Form 6 to restore their names on the electoral roll. Separately, in an affidavit dated October 26, the Commission denied any difference of opinion between the Chief Election Commissioner and the Election Commissioners over the SIR process, replying to a petition filed by INDIA bloc leaders led by Rahul Gandhi. The petitioners contend that the ECI has placed no material on record to substantiate its claim that the decision was unanimous, and have moved the top court for leave to serve interrogatories — written questions — on the Commission. The dispute is thus turning into a test of how far the internal decision-making of a constitutional body can be judicially scrutinised, alongside the safeguards available to an elector removed from the rolls.
stories.whyItMatters: It raises core GS-II questions on the autonomy and accountability of the Election Commission under Article 324, and on judicial review of an administrative body's internal deliberations. It also tests the legal safeguards an elector has when a name is deleted during roll revision.

perspectives.take: Frames the story around transparency and accountability, foregrounding Rahul Gandhi's argument that the ECI has produced no proof that the SIR decision was unanimous.
Legal-reporting lens: highlights the ECI's assurance that Form 6 applicants seeking restoration will not be prosecuted, a procedural-rights angle.
Focuses on the petitioners' procedural move in the Supreme Court — the plea for permission to serve interrogatories on the Election Commission.

static.topic: Supreme Court, High Courts and Judicial Review
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: Supreme Court, judicial review, writ jurisdiction
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Article 214) sit at the state level. Judicial review is the power of courts to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. Public interest litigation expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Articles 32 (Supreme Court) and 226 (High Courts) confer writ jurisdiction.
static.socioEconomic: Heavy pendency and judicial vacancies shape how quickly constitutional challenges to administrative action are resolved.
static.whyInNews: INDIA bloc leaders have moved the Supreme Court against the ECI's handling of the SIR, and now seek leave to serve interrogatories on the Commission.
static.wayForward: Courts must balance deference to an expert constitutional body with the need for a reasoned, reviewable record of its decisions.
prelimsPointers: Original jurisdiction over Centre-state disputes lies under Article 131.
Advisory jurisdiction is exercised under Article 143.
static.mainsAngle: Examine the scope of judicial review over the internal decision-making of constitutional bodies such as the Election Commission.

static.topic: Election Commission of India and Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Constitutional Bodies: Election Commission; electoral roll revision
static.whatIsIt: The ECI is a constitutional body under Article 324 charged with superintendence, direction and control of elections. Revision of electoral rolls is carried out under Section 21 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960; SIR is a constituency-wide, house-to-house verification exercise to purge rolls of dead, shifted and duplicate entries.
static.background: The ECI was established on 25 January 1950 and became a multi-member body in 1993 with two Election Commissioners alongside the CEC. In Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023) the Supreme Court prescribed a selection committee of the Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition and Chief Justice of India; the Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 replaced the CJI with a Union Cabinet Minister. SIR has been used for intensive house-to-house verification, most prominently in Bihar in 2025.
static.socioEconomic: Being on the electoral roll is widely used as proof of identity and residence, so deletions can have effects beyond the right to vote, particularly for the poor and internal migrants.
static.whyInNews: The ECI has told the Supreme Court that deleted voters who file Form 6 to restore their names will not face prosecution, while denying any rift within the Commission over the SIR.
static.wayForward: Publish a clear, reasoned record of revision decisions; strengthen notice, hearing and appeal mechanisms for affected electors; and ensure deletion is proportionate and documented.
prelimsPointers: Form 6 is the application for inclusion of a name in the electoral roll; Form 7 is for objections, Form 8 for corrections and Form 8A for transposition.
Section 21 of the RP Act, 1950 empowers special revision of electoral rolls; appeals against an ERO's decision lie to the Chief Electoral Officer and the ECI under Section 24.
The ECI became a three-member body in 1993, with the CEC and two Election Commissioners.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the constitutional safeguards around electoral roll revision and assess whether the present framework adequately protects an elector whose name is deleted.

prelims: Form 6 is used to apply for inclusion of a name in the electoral roll; Form 7 for objections to inclusion; Form 8 for correction; Form 8A for shifting within a constituency.
Special revision of electoral rolls is provided for under Section 21 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, read with the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.
The Election Commission is a constitutional body under Article 324 and has functioned as a three-member Commission since 1993.
Interrogatories are written questions administered to a party in a legal proceeding, answered on oath, and require the court's permission in writ proceedings.
stories.mainsQuestion: The credibility of the electoral roll is central to the integrity of elections. In the light of recent Special Intensive Revision exercises, examine the safeguards available to an elector whose name is deleted, and the institutional checks on the Election Commission's revision powers.

stories.headline: Manipur: Six abducted Liangmai Naga civilians laid to rest after 187 days
stories.summary: Six Liangmai Naga civilians who were abducted and killed in Manipur were finally interred in November 2026, 187 days after the incident, with the United Naga Council describing May 13, 2026 as the darkest day in the State's history. The interment came amid a statewide strike called over the killing of Naga civilians, during which police fired tear gas shells in Imphal. The episode has renewed attention on the unresolved Naga political question and on the hill-valley ethnic divide that has driven sustained violence in the State since 2023.
stories.whyItMatters: The story connects internal security in the North-East, the federal division of responsibility for law and order, and the stalled Naga peace process — recurring UPSC themes across GS-II and GS-III.

perspectives.take: Frames the event around delayed justice — bodies interred 187 days after abduction — and foregrounds the United Naga Council's characterisation of May 13, 2026 as Manipur's darkest day; a national, accountability-and-rights framing.

Leads with the law-and-order dimension — the statewide strike and tear gas firing in Imphal — highlighting the State's security response and the risk of wider disruption; a national daily with a governance-and-politics focus.

static.topic: Centre-State Relations and Internal Security in Manipur
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: India is a quasi-federal union: powers are divided between the Union and States via the Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Seventh Schedule), with residuary powers with the Union (Art. 248). 'Public order' and 'police' are State List subjects, while the Union has a constitutional duty under Article 355 to protect States against internal disturbance.
static.background: Sarkaria (1983) and Punchhi (2007) Commissions examined Centre-State balance. The Governor (Art. 153) is the Centre's constitutional representative and a flashpoint over assent to Bills (Art. 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Art. 201). In Manipur, prolonged ethnic conflict since 2023 has repeatedly tested the division of responsibility between the State government and the Union.
static.geography: Manipur is a landlocked hill-and-valley State bordering Myanmar; the Imphal valley is predominantly Meitei, while the surrounding hills are home to Naga and Kuki-Zo communities.
static.socioEconomic: Ethnic polarisation along hill-valley lines, displacement, blockade-driven supply disruptions and loss of livelihoods have deepened socio-economic distress.
static.whyInNews: Six Liangmai Naga civilians abducted and killed in May 2026 were interred in November 2026, and a statewide strike over the killing of Naga civilians saw tear gas shells fired in Imphal.
static.wayForward: Strengthen Centre-State coordination on security, ensure time-bound investigation, compensation and accountability, and pursue political dialogue with Naga and Kuki-Zo bodies alongside a hill-valley reconciliation process.
prelimsPointers: 'Public order' and 'police' are State List entries; the Union's duty to protect States from internal disturbance flows from Article 355.
Inter-State Council (Art. 263) is a recommendatory dispute-resolution body.
Concurrent List: union law prevails on repugnancy unless the state law is reserved for the President's assent (Art. 254).
static.mainsAngle: Ethnic conflict in the North-East tests both internal security capacity and the federal division of responsibility — examine whether the existing Centre-State framework is adequate for prolonged sub-national conflict.

static.topic: Ethnic Conflict and the Naga Question in the North-East
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Role of Non-State Actors; Linkages between Development and Extremism
static.whatIsIt: The Naga political question traces to the demand for a 'Greater Nagaland' (Nagalim) encompassing Naga-inhabited areas of Manipur, Assam and Arunachal Pradesh. The Naga ceasefire with the Government of India dates to 1997, and the United Naga Council (UNC) is the apex body of Naga tribes in Manipur.
static.background: The 1997 ceasefire between the Centre and NSCN-IM was extended to Manipur 'without territorial limits' in 2001, triggering large protests in Imphal and the burning of the State Assembly. Naga bodies in Manipur have since opposed State government moves on district reorganisation, and the hill-valley divide has sharpened further since the 2023 ethnic violence.
static.geography: Naga-inhabited districts of Manipur include Senapati, Ukhrul, Tamenglong, Chandel and Tengnoupal; the Liangmai are a Naga tribe of the Zeliangrong group.
static.socioEconomic: Hill communities have long complained of underdevelopment and political marginalisation relative to the Imphal valley, a grievance that fuels identity-based mobilisation.
static.whyInNews: The interment of six abducted Liangmai Naga civilians and the statewide strike over the killing of Naga civilians have renewed attention to the Naga question in Manipur.
static.wayForward: Conclusion of the Naga peace process with safeguards for Manipur's territorial integrity, coupled with equitable development and confidence-building measures for hill communities.
prelimsPointers: The Naga ceasefire with NSCN-IM dates to 1997; its 2001 extension to Manipur without territorial limits caused major unrest in Imphal.
The United Naga Council is an apex Naga tribal body in Manipur; the Liangmai are a Naga tribe of the Zeliangrong group.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how unresolved ethno-territorial demands in the North-East interact with internal security, governance and development policy.

prelims: Six Liangmai Naga civilians abducted and killed in Manipur were interred 187 days later, in November 2026.
A statewide strike in Manipur over the killing of Naga civilians saw police fire tear gas shells in Imphal.

stories.mainsQuestion: The persistence of ethnic violence in Manipur raises questions about both internal security capacity and the federal division of responsibility. Examine, with reference to the Naga question and the hill-valley divide.

stories.headline: Five EU states announce Rwanda 'return hub' for failed asylum seekers
stories.summary: Five EU member states — Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands — have jointly announced a 'return hub' in Rwanda for failed asylum seekers, according to BBC World. The facility is presented as a mechanism for removing migrants whose asylum claims have been rejected, rather than as an offshore processing centre for pending claims. It revives the third-country 'externalisation' model earlier attempted by the United Kingdom under its Rwanda partnership, which was discontinued in 2024. The move comes amid a broader European push to tighten asylum rules and accelerate deportations. Financing, legal safeguards and the precise role of Rwanda are yet to be specified.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the limits of the 1951 Refugee Convention's non-refoulement guarantee and the politics of responsibility-sharing in global refugee governance — core GS-II International Relations territory.

perspectives.take: Reports the announcement as a collective five-country EU initiative, framing it as a 'return hub' for failed asylum seekers and foregrounding the Rwanda precedent; Anglo-American wire framing stresses novelty and legality questions.

articles.title: Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda

static.topic: Externalisation of asylum and third-country 'return hubs'
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance; effect of policies of developed countries on India's interests
static.whatIsIt: Externalisation is the practice of shifting asylum processing, detention or removal to a third country so that states avoid hosting claimants on their own territory.
static.background: The UK–Rwanda Migration and Economic Development Partnership was announced in April 2022; the UK Supreme Court held the policy unlawful in November 2023 on non-refoulement grounds; Parliament then passed the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024; the scheme was discontinued by the incoming UK government in July 2024. Italy signed a protocol with Albania in November 2023 for offshore processing centres, which began operating in 2024. The EU Pact on Migration and Asylum was adopted in 2024, with application scheduled from 2026.
static.geography: Rwanda is a small, landlocked country in the Great Lakes region of East Africa, bordered by Uganda, Tanzania, Burundi and the Democratic Republic of the Congo; capital Kigali.
static.socioEconomic: Rwanda has positioned itself as a services and development hub in East Africa and is a member of the East African Community; host states typically cite development funding and job creation as benefits of such arrangements.
static.whyInNews: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands announced a joint 'return hub' in Rwanda for failed asylum seekers.
static.wayForward: Any such arrangement must satisfy non-refoulement, individualised assessment and an effective judicial remedy; sustainable alternatives lie in fairer intra-EU burden-sharing, expanded legal migration pathways and readmission agreements with origin countries.
keyTerms: EU Pact on Migration and Asylum
prelimsPointers: The UK's Rwanda asylum partnership was announced in 2022 and discontinued in 2024.
Italy's Albania protocol (2023) is the other prominent European offshore-processing model.
Rwanda is a member of the East African Community.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether third-country 'return hubs' are compatible with the principle of non-refoulement and the global refugee protection regime.

static.topic: UN refugee protection framework and UNHCR
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance; important international institutions
static.whatIsIt: The 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol define who is a refugee and codify non-refoulement; UNHCR, created in 1950, is the UN agency mandated to protect refugees.
static.background: The UN was founded in 1945 with six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members and ten elected members. UNHCR began operations in 1951 and its mandate was extended globally by the 1967 Protocol. The Global Compact on Refugees was adopted in 2018 to promote responsibility-sharing. India is a founding UN member, one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping, and has long sought permanent UNSC membership through the G4.
static.geography: UNHCR headquarters is in Geneva; the International Court of Justice sits at The Hague and UN headquarters is in New York.
static.socioEconomic: Refugee flows impose uneven costs on first-asylum states, most of them in the Global South, which underpins demands for equitable responsibility-sharing.
static.whyInNews: The EU 'return hub' plan in Rwanda tests the Convention's non-refoulement guarantee and the limits of responsibility-sharing.
static.wayForward: Strengthened multilateral responsibility-sharing, predictable financing for host states and expanded legal pathways are the reform options most often proposed.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent and 10 elected for two-year terms.
UNHCR was established in 1950 and began operations in 1951; headquarters in Geneva.
India is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how the externalisation of asylum challenges the UN's refugee protection architecture and what reforms would make responsibility-sharing effective.

static.topic: India–EU migration and mobility partnership
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India
static.whatIsIt: The India–EU Migration and Mobility Partnership, signed in 2016, provides a framework for legal migration, student and professional mobility, and cooperation on return and readmission.
static.background: India has signed migration and mobility partnership agreements with the EU and with several individual European states. The EU is a major destination for Indian students, professionals and the wider diaspora, whose remittances are an important external sector support. India–EU relations are anchored in annual summits, the Trade and Technology Council and ongoing free trade negotiations.
static.socioEconomic: Tighter EU asylum and return policies can affect Indian students, workers and irregular migrants, and can shape remittance flows and the bargaining space in mobility negotiations.
static.whyInNews: The five-country EU 'return hub' announcement signals a hardening of European migration policy that could influence India–EU mobility talks.
static.wayForward: India should press for transparent, rules-based mobility pathways and consular safeguards for its nationals while negotiating readmission commitments.
prelimsPointers: The India–EU Migration and Mobility Partnership was signed in 2016.
The EU is among the largest destinations for Indian students and skilled professionals.
static.mainsAngle: How should India balance readmission obligations with protection of its diaspora in the context of hardening European migration policies?

prelims: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands jointly announced a 'return hub' in Rwanda for failed asylum seekers (reported November 2026).
Rwanda is a landlocked East African Community member state with its capital at Kigali.
The principle of non-refoulement under the 1951 Refugee Convention bars returning refugees to territories where they face serious threats.
The UK's own Rwanda asylum partnership, announced in 2022, was discontinued in 2024.
stories.mainsQuestion: Third-country 'return hubs' are being promoted as a solution to irregular migration in Europe. Examine their compatibility with the principle of non-refoulement and suggest a rights-based framework for international responsibility-sharing.

stories.headline: India, Egypt set 90-day target to launch trade agreement talks
stories.summary: India and Egypt have agreed on a 90-day target for commencing negotiations on a bilateral trade agreement, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. The proposed pact is intended to deepen commercial ties, streamline payment settlement between the two economies, and open up cooperation in sectors such as shipbuilding and seaports. The move builds on the strategic partnership the two countries elevated in 2023 and on India's wider push to expand its network of trade agreements. Egypt's control of the Suez Canal and its position as a gateway to Africa and the Mediterranean give the engagement added strategic weight.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests understanding of India's FTA strategy, external-sector priorities such as rupee-based settlement, and the West Asia–Africa dimension of Indian foreign policy — relevant to GS-II International Relations and GS-III Economy.
